blocks.text: Pattern is presented as the first book devoted to a Mauritanian studio photographer: Amadou Fall, who portrayed the people of Nouadhibou at his Studio Grand Fall from the 1960s onward.
By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Amadou Fall

“Pushing open the door of Studio Grand Fall meant leaving the street behind. The dust stayed outside. The noise too,” writes photographer Adrien Tache. Amadou Fall’s son entrusted Tache with bringing the archive to life, after decades of leaving it untouched. Nomadic families, city dwellers, Spanish migrants, merchants and officials all sat in front of his lens. Together they form a collective portrait of an Atlantic port where North Africa, West Africa and Europe met.

The clothes in Fall’s portraits tell that same story. For a long time, Mauritanian dress favoured plain or indigo-dyed cottons. Then came wax prints: cottons whose bold, colourful patterns are created by using wax to resist the dye. Dutch and British factories first produced them in imitation of Indonesian batik, intending to sell them in Asia. It was in West Africa, however, that they found their public during the nineteenth century, as traders and their customers gave each motif a name of their own, linked to marriage, wealth, migration or independence.

Rather than replacing traditional garments, wax cloth was integrated into existing ways of dressing, and by the 1960s it had become a sign of modernity and aspiration. That same cloth now binds the book: each copy is covered in a different wax fabric printed in West Africa, echoing the patterns some of the sitters could have been wearing.
The book Pattern is published by Fraglich Publishing and available for 35 Euro.
